title: The good question
hook: in the study hall a sharp question earns more respect than a quick answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, chavruta: two people, one book, arguing out loud as friends. Your line was learn with a partner. Did anyone push back on you? Day one hundred fifty-two.

There's a story people often tell about a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, Isidor Rabi. He grew up in a Jewish immigrant family in New York. Other kids came home from school, he said, and their mothers asked: what did you learn today? His mother asked something else. Izzy, did you ask a good question today? He said that question made him a scientist. Whether every detail happened just that way, nobody can check. But Jews keep telling it, because it sounds exactly right. In a study hall, the person everyone turns to isn't the one with the fastest answer. It's the one who raises a hand and says: wait. That doesn't make sense.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU LEARN TODAY?` → `DID YOU ASK A GOOD QUESTION?` → `WAIT. THAT DOESN'T MAKE SENSE.`

segments.voice: Open the Mishnah, the first great book of Jewish law, to its very first line. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts with a question: from what time may the Shema be said in the evening? The whole Talmud grows from there, and page after page, its engine is the question. The Aramaic word is kushya, a difficulty. A student notices two verses that seem to disagree, or a rule that doesn't fit, and says so. The Talmud doesn't hide these. It lines them up and works on them, sometimes for pages. Sometimes the answer never comes, and the Talmud says so plainly: teiku, let it stand. Some later readers heard in that word a hope that Elijah the prophet would one day come and settle it. Until then, the question stays on the table, honored. The rabbis also taught that a shy person can't learn. That's from Pirkei Avot: someone too embarrassed to ask will stay where they are. And every year at the Passover seder, the youngest child stands up and asks: why is this night different from all other nights? The whole story of the Exodus is told as an answer to a child's question. So what makes a question good? It's real: you actually want to know. It's close to the text: it points at a word, not a vague feeling. And it's brave: it risks sounding like you missed something. A quick answer ends the conversation. A good question starts it.
screen: `THE MISHNAH OPENS WITH A QUESTION.` · `KUSHYA: A DIFFICULTY, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `TEIKU: LET IT STAND.` · `A SHY PERSON CAN'T LEARN.` · then, large: `ASK BETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one real question. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been told so often you stopped asking about it: a rule at work, a family habit, a line you've heard all your life. Now ask one honest question about it. Not a complaint. A question you'd actually like answered. Turn it until it's sharp and short. When the bell ends, write it down. The bell holds the time.
The good question. In the study hall, it earns more respect than a quick answer, because it's where learning begins.
Your line: ask better. Today, when someone tells you something, ask one real question before you answer. Day one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Jewish study, students are expected to raise difficulties with the text out loud, and the Talmud records unresolved questions rather than hiding them; at the Passover seder, children ask the Four Questions.

fork.setup: you're new in the study hall. the teacher reads a line that seems to contradict one from last week. what do you do?
options: stay quiet so you don't look slow.
say it out loud: these two don't fit.
assume you misremembered and move on.
fork.reveal: you raise it. a kushya, a difficulty said out loud, is how the Talmud moves, and a shy person, Avot says, can't learn.

original.note: Aramaic: a difficulty, the hard question the Talmud raises and works on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good question is one that has an easy answer.
what it means: a real, precise, brave question about the text, which in the study hall earns more respect than a quick reply.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 opens 'me'eimatai', from when; the Talmud's kushya and teiku; Avot 2:5, 'lo habayshan lamed', the bashful does not learn.

notes: The I. I. Rabi anecdote is widely retold (e.g. in a 1988 letter/interview); the script frames it as a story people tell and says the details can't be checked. Confirm the framing.

Teiku: the folk reading as an acronym for 'Tishbi yetaretz kushyot ve'iba'yot' (Elijah will resolve difficulties) is later and not the word's etymology; the script says 'some later readers heard in that word a hope'. Confirm.
Avot 2:5 numbering (2:5 or 2:6 depending on edition).
Script paraphrases the Four Questions; confirm that 'the youngest child' is the usual custom to cite.
